title: Projected droughts readily trigger vegetation decline
authors: Zixu Jia; Tao Lin; Xiangzhong Guo; Faith Ka Shun Chan; Lichang Yin; Hongkai Geng; Yicheng Zheng; Junmao Zhang; Yuan Chen; Meixia Lin; Jing Lin; Yuqin Liu
abstract: Drought is intensifying under a warming climate, while the lag of vegetation response and the drought trigger thresholds for relative vegetation loss remain insufficiently quantified. Here we provide a global assessment of vegetation responses to the Terrestrial Water Storage Drought Severity Index (TWS_DSI) under historical and future climate scenarios. Using five vegetation indicators, including Leaf Area Index (LAI), Fraction of Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FPAR), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (kNDVI), and Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), we quantified their lagged responses to drought during the historical period. The mean optimal lag times ranged from 8.20 months for LAI to 10.59 months for NDVI, with FPAR (8.78 months), GPP (9.80 months), and kNDVI (10.42 months) showing intermediate lag responses. Based on future LAI simulations under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, the mean lag varied from 5.15 to 10.48 months. At predefined vegetation loss levels (≤40 th , ≤30 th , ≤20 th , ≤10 th ), we identified the drought trigger thresholds for vegetation decline and mapped their spatial variability. Compared to the historical baseline, the average drought trigger thresholds increased by 30.0%, 36.3%, and 35.3% under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, respectively, indicating heightened vulnerability whereby even milder drought conditions in the future could trigger vegetation decline. Our findings characterize the temporal lags, threshold behavior, and projected changes of vegetation responses to terrestrial water deficits, providing a scientific basis for assessing ecosystem vulnerability and informing targeted ecological conservation and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Long-term, national-scale records of landslide persistence and dynamic hazard in a mountain landscape
authors: Erin L. Harvey; Nick J. Rosser; Mark Kincey; Alexander Logan Densmore; Tzu‐Hsin Karen Chen; Megh Raj Dhital; Karen C. Seto; Gopi Krishna Basyal; Tom R. Robinson; Ram Shrestha; Katie J. Oven; Katherine Arrell
abstract: Abstract As mountain populations grow and exposure to hazard increases, understanding the dynamic hazard posed by landslides is essential. However, our ability to constrain landslide hazard is limited by relatively few good-quality datasets that are often collected across small geographical areas. These datasets typically focus on specific triggering events, such as earthquakes or rainstorms, further complicating assessments of landslide hazard through time. To better capture landslide hazard through space and time, long-term datasets over large extents are needed. Here, we analyse a 22-year record of landslide occurrence to decipher the dynamic nature of the hazard posed by landslides in Nepal. We find that recurrent or persistent landslides dominate national-scale patterns of landsliding, accounting for c. 80% of all visible landslides at any given point in time. Of new landslide areas, only half occurred in locations >30 m away from other landslides. These findings emphasise the importance of also considering pre-existing landslides when assessing hazard. Individual triggering events, including both earthquakes and rainfall, leave a distinctive footprint visible at the national scale in metrics such as landslide density, persistence, and recurrence. Such metrics add significant value to multi-temporal landslide inventories and provide a basis for mitigation efforts, particularly where resources are limited.

title: Global climate impact of land-surface change driven by radiative effects
authors: Philipp de Vrese; Victor A. Brovkin; Moritz Günther; Sarah M. Kang; Thomas Raddatz; Wim Thiery; Yi Yao
abstract: Abstract A robust proportionality between radiative forcing and global-mean temperature has been established for most climate drivers. However, land-surface changes are considered an exception due to their potential to alter surface hydrology, introducing non-radiative effects that may rival those from surface albedo changes. Here, comparing Earth-system-model simulations with large-scale perturbations of surface albedo and water availability, we find that the spatially integrated biophysical climate impact is similarly dominated by radiative processes and scales approximately linearly with the resulting shifts in planetary albedo, implying a ~ 0.4 K surface temperature response per W m −2 change in top-of-atmosphere net short-wave radiation. Thus, while non-radiative effects strongly influence local temperatures, their net contribution to the global-mean signal is negligible. The planetary-albedo response is primarily governed by regional cloud-cover characteristics, resulting in a substantially stronger temperature response to land-surface change in mid- and high-latitude regions than in the tropics and subtropics.

title: Aridity-driven shifts in plant–microbial diversity relationships across the arid and semi-arid grasslands of northern China
authors: Congwen Wang; Heqi Wang; Hong Yang; Wei Qiang; Changxing Fu; Jiayan Fan; Yingxin Huang
abstract: Abstract Climate change-driven aridification threatens above- and belowground biodiversity, yet how the relationships between plant diversity and soil microbial diversity change along aridity gradients remains unclear. Here, we conducted a 4,000-km field survey across arid and semi-arid grasslands in northern China. We show that soil conditions, plant diversity, and microbial diversity exhibit sequential threshold responses along the aridity gradient. Beyond these thresholds, plant, bacterial, and fungal diversity generally decline, whereas archaeal species diversity increases. As aridity increases, the negative effects of soil salinity on plant, bacterial, and fungal diversity become stronger, whereas soil salinity shows increasingly positive associations with archaeal species diversity. Plant–bacteria and plant–fungi diversity relationships strengthen in drier regions, whereas plant–archaea relationships become decoupled. These findings show that aridity acts as a strong environmental filter, selecting stress-tolerant species and restructuring plant–microbial diversity coupling in a taxon-specific manner, and highlight the importance of aridity-dependent biodiversity coupling for shaping ecosystem resilience in arid and semi-arid grasslands under ongoing aridification.

title: Ultrahigh discharge voltage plateau of 3.2 V achieved in Li-CO 2 batteries using iron polyphthalocyanine
authors: Ning Zhao; Yi Zhang; Li-Min Liu; Han-Qi Zhang; Zheng Meng; Shujiang Ding; Qiang Wang; Xiaofei Hu
abstract: Rechargeable lithium-carbon dioxide (Li-CO 2 ) batteries offer great potential for greenhouse gas use and high-energy-density storage. However, their practical application is hindered by the formation of a thermodynamically stable Li 2 CO 3 (lithium carbonate) product that is hard to decompose during charging. Highly crystalline and conductive reticular material iron polyphthalocyanine (pFe II Pc) as a solid-state redox mediator into Li-CO 2 batteries tailors the cathode reaction pathway, enabling stable Li 2 C 2 O 4 (lithium oxalate) generation and an extraordinary discharge plateau of 3.2 V beyond the theoretical limit. Beyond delivering an ultrahigh discharge capacity of 28,790 milliampere-hours per gram and reversible cyclability over 1400 hours (cutoff capacity of 1000 milliampere-hours per gram) at 100 milliamperes per gram, the Li-CO 2 batteries exhibit excellent temperature adaptability (−40 to 80°C). The Li-CO 2 pouch cells using pFe II Pc as the solid-state redox mediator achieve a high energy density of 678 watt-hours per kilogram on the basis of total device mass and maintain reversible cycling for 251 hours. Our work pioneers a promising pathway toward practical high-efficiency Li-CO 2 batteries.

title: Switchable quantum dot photoluminescence across a broad spectrum with all-visible-light activated diarylethene photoswitches
authors: Lin Xi; Kezhou Chen; Shuai Zhang; Taibin Wang; 刘铁根 Liu Tiegen; Bo Albinsson; Lili Hou
abstract: Abstract Precise and reversible photoluminescence switching is highly attractive for optical memory, bioimaging, and smart displays. However, achieving broadband photoluminescence modulation through a simple and general strategy remains challenging, while the ultraviolet light requirement of most molecular photoswitches limits practical applications. Here, we achieve all-visible-light activated reversible photoluminescence modulation of quantum dots across an ultrawide spectral range of nearly 500 nm from blue to near-infrared region using diarylethene photoswitches. In the ring-open form of diarylethenes, quantum dots emitting blue, green, red, white and near-infrared light remain in the photoluminescence on-state. Under 405 nm irradiation, diarylethenes undergo ring-closure through triplet sensitization by CdS quantum dots, resulting in significant photoluminescence quenching to the off-state, with the maximum efficiency of 99.6% and an on/off ratio up to 250. Green-light irradiation reverses the diarylethenes back to the ring-open form, fully restoring the photoluminescence on-state. Our approach further enables reversible multi-level data storage and near-infrared anti-counterfeiting, highlighting the potential for smart light-responsive materials and optoelectronic devices.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals microenvironmental heterogeneity in osteoarthritic subchondral bone
authors: Weiqiang Lin; Xinyi Xiao; Di Tian; Yun Gong; Lei Huang; Woong‐Ki Kim; Md Ariful Islam; Guihua Pan; Binghao Zou; Zhe Luo; Qing Tian; William Sherman; Fernando Sánchez; Austin Ross; Chuan Qiu
abstract: Although increasing evidence implicates subchondral bone alterations in osteoarthritis, the spatial organization of subchondral bone remodeling remains unclear. Applying spatial transcriptomics to human subchondral bone, we identify a spatially conserved osteogenic core-halo architecture that displays transcriptional reprogramming in sclerotic microenvironments. Spatial dependency and a customized cell-cell communication framework reveal disrupted osteoblast-osteoclast spatial coupling, enhanced osteoblast-mesenchymal interactions, and identify FN1-SDC2 and COL1A1-DDR2 as candidate stromal-osteogenic signaling axes that may contribute to aberrant bone remodeling. Additionally, we present the in situ transcriptional landscape of osteocytes and reveal its potential regulatory role in aberrant bone remodeling. We further delineate a continuum of spatial ecotypes exhibiting distinct enrichment, spatial topology reorganization, and inter-ecotype communication rewiring across pathological states. Metabolic flux inference additionally reveals substrate-limited, stressed states across multiple ecotypes in sclerotic microenvironments. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in osteoarthritis and offer a valuable framework for future mechanistic studies and therapeutic exploration. Subchondral bone remodeling is increasingly implicated in osteoarthritis, but its spatial organization remain incompletely understood. This study provides a high-resolution spatial map of subchondral bone and identifies conserved spatial architectures, revealing distinct microenvironmental states and candidate signaling pathways associated with subchondral bone sclerosis.

title: Single-photon controlled phase shifts with colloidal quantum dots at room temperature
authors: Chai Hu; Wenyi Dai; Yuanyuan Zhou; Haiyu Xu; Jiefei Liu; X X Xu
abstract: Quantum logic gates based on quantum electrodynamics (QED) in strong coupling regime between quantum dots and microcavities are key elements for scalable quantum computing and all-optical quantum networks. Here, a single colloidal quantum dot was site-selectively positioned onto a dielectric photonic crystal hybrid microcavity using a soft nanoprobe technique, enabling the study of strong coupling between the colloidal quantum dots and bound states in the continuum in the cavity. By combining photoluminescence spectroscopy, Michelson interferometry, and continuous-wave pump-probe technology, the wavelength- and power-dependent phase shifts were systematically characterized. Controlled π-phase shifts of a single photon were experimentally demonstrated in both single colloidal quantum dot and high-concentration colloidal quantum dots coupled microcavity systems. This work provides an experimental basis for the development of room temperature quantum optoelectronic devices, including quantum phase gates and ultralow power optical switches.

title: S -Nitrosylation of glycogen phosphorylase regulates nuclear glycogenolysis and is impaired in metabolic liver disorders
authors: Leandro R. Soria; Alfonso Manuel D’Alessio; Vincenzo Casertano; Elena Polishchuk; Andrea Pasquadibisceglie; Iolanda Boffa; Anna Diana; Rossella De Cegli; Lucia De Stefano; Edoardo Nusco; Paola Arena; Matteo Audano; Nico Mitro; Tsuyoshi Morita; Otto Baba
abstract: Nuclear glycogen storage has been known for nearly 100 years. However, its role in diseases remains unclear. Here, we found nuclear glycogen storage in livers of mice and humans with argininosuccinic aciduria (ASA), an inborn error of metabolism. Nuclear glycogenolysis sustains histone acetylation and liver homeostasis. We show that hepatic nuclear glycogenolysis is regulated by nitric oxide (NO)–dependent control of the nuclear abundance of liver glycogen phosphorylase (PYGL), an enzyme involved in glycogen breakdown that translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus. In vivo, NO supplementation restored the nuclear content of PYGL by promoting its S -nitrosylation at cysteine-446 and its nuclear translocation. Next, we found that nuclear import of PYGL is mediated by HNRNPF, a regulator of RNA maturation that shuttles between the nucleus and cytosol, thus linking control of gene expression to RNA metabolism. Similar changes were detected in both rodent and human livers with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a global health concern with limited therapies, that shares with ASA a decrease in NO synthesis. In conclusion, our findings reveal a mechanism underlying reduced glycogenolysis and hepatic nuclear glycogen storage disorders, a new group of metabolic disorders.

title: Precise molecular sieving in polycrystalline covalent organic framework membranes
authors: Xiansong Shi; Haipei Shao; Xin Zhang; Fen Huang; Q Z Liu; He Li; Wei Juan Zhao; Junyu Ren; 蒲云川; Wen-Hua Li; Nengxiu Zhu; Ming Lin; Dan Zhao
abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) unlock opportunities to unite rapid mass transport with molecular-level sieving through membranes. However, achieving long-range crystallographic order within these membranes remains a central challenge that limits their separation precision. Here, we report a monomer-driven strategy for the ambient-condition fabrication of COF polycrystalline membranes featuring definite lattice order and polyhedral textures, reminiscent of benchmark metal-organic framework counterparts. Using a rigid, π-conjugated pyrene-centered tetraamine, we enable nonepitaxial intergrowth of faceted COF crystals on a porous support, yielding a 350-nanometer-thick membrane with a record-high Brunauer-Emmett-Teller surface area of 2121 square meters per gram among COF separation membranes of comparable pore size. The resulting COF membrane preserves its crystallographic order and polyhedral texture even after 1 month of solvent exposure while uniquely combining increased surface stiffness with high tensile ductility. Notably, we demonstrate its superior liquid-phase molecular selectivity, outperforming COF analogs with considerably smaller pore apertures, and elucidate an unambiguous correlation between crystallographic order and permselectivity. This work positions crystallographic ordering as a guiding principle for COF membranes, opening more possibilities at the intersection of framework materials and separation technologies.

title: Improving large-scale river routing models with ESA long-term CCI discharge data assimilation: advancing accuracy for climate studies
authors: Malak Sadki; Gaëtan Noual; Simon Munier; Vanessa Pedinotti; Kaushlendra Verma; Clément Albergel; Sylvain Biancamaria; Alice Andral
abstract: Abstract. Large scale hydrological models like CTRIP and MGB are essential for simulating river dynamics and supporting large-scale climate studies. Their accuracy can be significantly improved through satellite data assimilation. This study leverages 20 years of high-resolution discharge data (2000–2020) from the ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) to enhance CTRIP and MGB models via ensemble Kalman Filter frameworks (HyDAS and HYFAA). Applied to the Niger and Congo basins, the models assimilate discharge data derived from altimetry and multispectral imagery, alongside water surface elevation (WSE) anomaly data, to evaluate their impact on model performance. Discharge assimilation was more effective than WSE anomaly assimilation, as it provided a more direct input for improving model accuracy. Temporal data density was the key factor in reducing bias and enhancing the simulation of seasonal flow patterns, with spatial coverage and data quality also playing important roles. In the Niger Basin, the assimilation of denser discharge data resulted in a significant bias reduction, which should improve the representation of long-term climate trends. Furthermore, the higher temporal resolution allowed for better capture of flow variability, which is crucial for both seasonal climate studies and short-term predictions, such as extreme hydrological events. The study also emphasizes the trade-offs between data resolution and quality, particularly in the Congo Basin. Future advancements include merging altimetry and multispectral discharge data, improving the discharge retrieval algorithms using SWOT data, and refining data assimilation techniques to improve climate studies and river system modeling in complex, climate-impacted basins.

title: Cationic chain-anchored monolayer enables wide-temperature composite polymer electrolytes for lithium-metal batteries
authors: Qimin Peng; Yong Chen; Jiajun Gong; Haojie Xu; Taolue Wen; Mengyu Liu; Shunshun Zhao; Yu Han; Dongfang Li; Shijian Wang; Robin Wang; Doron Aurbach; Guoxiu Wang; Shimou Chen
abstract: Ionic transport pathways critically influence the stability, capacity, and safety of solid-state lithium-metal batteries. However, realizing efficient ionic conduction that couples fast ion transport kinetics with interfacial stability remains a formidable challenge in solid-state lithium-metal batteries under wide-temperature conditions. Here, we report a cationic chain-anchored monolayer strategy for engineering stable ion transport pathways within poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene)/garnet-based composite polymer electrolytes. The dynamic evolution is investigated using synchrotron infrared spectroscopy, two-dimensional solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and additional operando measurements. We demonstrate that an in-situ formed single-ion-like conducting cationic chain-anchored monolayer, featuring solvent-phobic chain-tethered cationic channels, establishes robust and efficient ion transport pathways in the composite electrolyte interface. The resultant electrolytes deliver a low activation energy (0.092 eV) and high Li+ transference number (0.78), enabling 400 cycles at 120 °C (Li||LiFePO4, >99% capacity retention) and 450 cycles at −25 °C (4.5 V Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2, 82.5% capacity retention). Our work offers an effective strategy towards quasi-solid/solid-state lithium-metal batteries with stable long-term cycling across a wide-temperature range. Solid-state lithium-metal batteries are promising candidates for high-energy-density energy storage yet suffer from severe interfacial and ion-transport limitations under wide-temperature. Herein, authors propose a cationic chain-anchored monolayer strategy to construct stable ion transport pathways with robust wide-temperature performance (−25 to 120 °C).

title: A large-scale molecular dynamics investigation of anisotropic hydraulic conductivity in compacted clay system
authors: Yu Zhong; Annan Zhou; Jiapei Du; A. Zaoui
abstract: This study developed a large-scale molecular dynamics framework to investigate anisotropic hydraulic conductivity by linking directional water transport to compaction state, platelet fabric, and surface chemistry. A total of 150 multi-particle nanoflow models were constructed across dry densities ( ρ d ) of 1.2–1.8 g·cm −3 , orientational order parameters ( S ) of 0.60 to 0.92, and cation exchange capacities (CEC) of 0.11–97.44 cmol·kg −1 . Simulated hydraulic conductivities ranged from 0.77 × 10 -14 to 1.96 × 10 -12 m·s −1 , with 97.0% of available experimental measurements falling within this envelope. Mean horizontal hydraulic conductivity ( k h ) consistently exceeded mean vertical hydraulic conductivity ( k v ) by factors of approximately 2.4–5.6. Increasing dry density narrowed water-accessible pores, reduced independent spanning pathways and critical spanning diameters, and increased tortuosity, thereby decreasing both k h and k v . Platelet orientation differentiated the two flow directions by maintaining more direct horizontal pathways. Increasing CEC shifted pore water toward Na associated states and reduced the flux carried by interfacial only and free water, further lowering both k h and k v . Random Forest models achieved mean testing R 2 values of 0.92 for k h and 0.88 for k v and identified dry density as the dominant descriptor in both directions. Platelet orientation had a greater relative influence on vertical than horizontal conductivity, whereas CEC made a smaller but consistent contribution. Fixed-density sensitivity analysis showed that increasing dry density shifted the relative sensitivity weight from platelet orientation toward CEC, particularly for k v . These findings clarify the distinct structural and physicochemical controls on directional water transport and hydraulic anisotropy in compacted clay barriers.

title: Watershed‐Scale Simulation of Hydrology and Carbon Cycling With Explicit Lake Representation
authors: J. Z. Liu; Wanhong Yang; J. S. Xu; Y. Q. Liu; J. C. Jiang; Junzhi Liu
abstract: Abstract Lakes play a key role in regulating watershed hydrology and carbon transport, yet their effects are often simplified or omitted in hydrological‐biogeochemical models. This limitation is particularly evident in lake‐dominated basins, where lake can alter downstream water and carbon export. Here, we extend the Watershed‐based Integrated Simulator for the Environment (WISE) into a lake‐explicit framework that represents lake boundaries, river‐lake connectivity, lake‐local contributing areas, and hydrological‐biogeochemical processes. The model was applied to the Lake basin and evaluated using watershed outlet discharge, and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) observations at lake inflow and outflow locations. The model captured the main hydrological and DOC dynamics, with daily discharge KGE values of 0.65 and 0.64, and DOC KGE values calculated at discrete sampling dates ranging from 0.52 to 0.74 during calibration and validation, respectively. Simulations showed that lake modified watershed water and DOC transport by delaying downstream transmission, attenuating daily variability, and weakening concentration‐discharge relationships. The lake reduced annual variability of water and DOC fluxes by more than 50% in most years and reduced the DOC concentration‐discharge slope from 0.93 at inflow to 0.26 at outflow. Counterfactual scenarios showed that representing the lake as a river reach without recalibration altered the magnitude and timing of downstream DOC export relative to the lake‐explicit model. Although recalibration dampened some of the variability, the river‐reach representation still failed to reproduce the combination of peak attenuation and sustained release simulated by the lake‐explicit model. These results highlight explicit lake representation as a key direction for watershed DOC modeling.

title: Watershed Characteristics Modulate the Global Response of Fractional Evapotranspiration to Wet Climate Extremes
authors: Maheshwari Neelam
abstract: Abstract Intensifying wet extremes under continued warming threaten water security and ecosystem functioning by perturbing land–atmosphere water fluxes. Yet, the watershed‐scale controls on how wet‐event intensity and duration translate into changes in fractional evapotranspiration (fET) remain poorly constrained at global scales. Here, using monthly wet climate extreme indices (CEIs) and fET across ∼986 global watersheds, we quantify CEI–fET coupling and attribute its spatial variability to watershed properties using Random Forest models and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Across event types, soil organic carbon (SOC) and groundwater table depth (GWT) consistently structure coupling regimes, indicating a robust role for soil state and subsurface storage. However, the dominant texture axis differs by extreme type: intensity‐based extremes are most strongly organized by SOC–GWT–clay regimes, consistent with pulse retention and buffering, whereas duration‐based extremes are organized by SOC–GWT–silt regimes and permafrost‐related constraints, consistent with persistence‐driven drainage and saturation sensitivity. Supported SHAP‐transition analysis identifies data‐constrained regime boundaries. Lagged correlations further reveal multi‐timescale behavior: coupling varies at short lags but tends to shift toward negative associations at longer lags, especially for duration‐based extremes. In a permafrost‐limited subset, vegetation state and topography become more prominent predictors, highlighting how cold‐region constraints alter which attributes dominate. Together, these results provide a globally consistent diagnostic framework for identifying watershed regimes where intensifying wet extremes are more likely to yield sustained evapotranspiration responses versus reduced fET sensitivity. By quantifying regime thresholds, the study offers a diagnostic framework that may inform targeted mitigation strategies and policy frameworks, such as IPCC adaptation guidelines.

title: Varying Seasonal Runoff Drives the Timing and Volume of Water‐Dependent Recreational Activities in the Sacramento‐San Joaquin Delta
authors: Jeffrey S. Jenkins; Isaac Sanchez Terrazas; Laurel G. Larsen; Daniel R. Cayan; Yu Cai; Brett Milligan
abstract: Abstract Climate variations affect access to recreational opportunities through different mechanisms that influence the provisioning of water and ecosystem services. From 2000 to 2022, Northern and Central California experienced extreme climate fluctuations, with alternating multi‐year dry spells and wet years causing highly variable runoff from the Sierra Nevada into the Sacramento‐San Joaquin Delta. This study assesses how these hydroclimatic variations influence regional recreation by analyzing summer activities (boating, day use) alongside winter activities (birding, waterfowl hunting) at state parks and wildlife areas. The objective is to evaluate how monthly visitor volume and timing shift during drought versus wet conditions, distinguishing between activities directly or indirectly dependent on water resources. During summer droughts with critical low runoff, recreational activity declines sharply; boating drops by 65.8% and day use decreases by 13.8% at state park units. Conversely, winter droughts correlate with increased recreational engagement. Critical low runoff is associated with a 23.4% increase in birding observations and a 50.2% increase in waterfowl hunting takes. This winter increase occurs because restricted wetland resources concentrate waterfowl populations, making them more accessible to visitors. Activities directly dependent on water resources, including recreational fisheries, show the highest sensitivity to runoff fluctuations. We also find that visitor spending is highest during critical drought and wet runoff extremes, reflecting winter demand in drought years, and summer demand in the wettest years. These results highlight the vulnerability of water‐dependent recreation and its economic contributions as climate change accelerates the frequency and magnitude of extreme wet and dry cycles.

title: Time‐Varying Operation Policies With GRU‐Based Parameterization for Adaptive Multi‐Objective Reservoir Operation Under Climate Change
authors: Yiming Wei; Renchao Wang; Lu Zhuo; Zengchuan Dong
abstract: Abstract Designing reservoir operation policies that can adapt to non‐stationary hydroclimatic conditions is a major challenge for water resources management under climate change. This study develops an adaptive dynamic operation policy (ADOP), in which Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) are coupled with a gated recurrent unit (GRU)‐based parameterization module that maps meteorological information to time‐varying RBF weights. Using the reservoir system in the Qingjiang River Basin, China, as a case study, ADOP is optimized using an expanded historical hydroclimatic ensemble within an evolutionary multi‐objective direct policy search (EMODPS) framework and is evaluated under both an independent historical test period and 12 GCM‐based climate scenarios. A static operation policy (SOP) and a scenario‐specific re‐optimized ideal operation policy (IOP) are used as benchmarks. Results show that ADOP outperforms SOP under both historical training and test conditions. Under future scenarios, ADOP achieves higher hypervolume than SOP in 10 of 12 scenarios, indicating the advantage of the time‐varying parameterization in out‐of‐sample conditions. Although both historically trained policies retain a performance gap relative to the re‐optimized IOP, ADOP partially mitigates this gap. The water‐level and release trajectories for representative years further demonstrate that the advantage of ADOP is associated with improved storage–release coordination. Moreover, a diagnostic comparison supports the value of the GRU‐based module, as adding meteorological inputs to a static RBF policy does not reproduce ADOP's gains. The proposed time‐varying policy provides a practical pathway for improving the adaptability of historically trained reservoir operation policies under uncertain future hydroclimatic conditions.

title: Structure–Function Coherent Coarsening for Cross‐Resolution Ecohydrological Modeling
authors: Long Jiang; Yang Yang; Morgan Thornwell; Robert McKane; Sonali Chokshi; Huan‐Feng Duan; Tiantian Yang; Hoshin V. Gupta
abstract: Abstract Ecohydrological models are increasingly applied in regional scenario‐based studies, yet their cross‐resolution application remains constrained by high computational costs of fine‐resolution simulations and by structural inconsistencies introduced during scale transfer. We propose a Structure–Function Coherent Coarsening (SFCC) framework that improves the preservation of hydrological structure and functional heterogeneity during model input coarsening. Using the VELMA model in 24 subbasins of the Salish Sea Basin, USA, we evaluate coarsening strategies for three input types: (a) DEMs coarsened with a Hydro‐Aware approach that better preserves drainage topology; (b) land cover and soil type data sets coarsened with function‐preserving methods ( Auto‐Weight and Auto‐Reassign ) that retain small but process‐dominant classes; and (c) initial conditions coarsened with Hydro‐Aware , Landcover‐Aware , and Soil‐Aware strategies to improve temporal stability. Results show that the Hydro‐Aware method better preserves watershed morphology and yields more consistent runoff and nitrate loss predictions across resolutions than mean‐based coarsening. For categorical inputs, the function‐preserving methods can reduce the dominant‐class bias of majority aggregation, particularly in basins where small, high‐impact patches drive nitrogen export. Long‐term simulations show that hydrological variables stabilize quickly, whereas biogeochemical variables stabilize more slowly. In both cases, differences caused by coarsening decrease over time and eventually level off. This suggests that preserving both structural consistency and functional heterogeneity can help maintain stable model behavior over time. By operating directly at the data‐input level, SFCC improves integration of multi‐source data sets while retaining high‐resolution information. It supports cross‐scale simulation, calibration, and model integration, and provides a scalable foundation for regional scenario analysis.

title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Active Root Zone Storage Revealed From Hybrid Machine Learning
authors: Georgios Blougouras; Shijie Jiang; Alexander Brenning; Mirco Migliavacca; Louise J. Slater; Jialiang Zhou; Rohini Kumar; Lu Tian; Chao Wang; Markus Reichstein
abstract: Abstract Water within the root zone regulates water, energy, and carbon exchanges at the land‐atmosphere interface, yet the dynamically active portion of subsurface water that ecosystems mobilize for evapotranspiration (ET) remains unclear, because it represents only part of the total subsurface storage. To address this gap, we develop a catchment‐scale, ecosystem‐oriented hybrid machine learning model that integrates a parsimonious ecohydrological structure with data‐driven flexibility to infer time‐varying active root zone storage (a S rz ) as a latent state variable. Without prescribing rooting depth or soil layers, the model learns adaptive water partitioning from multi‐source observations of ET, runoff, snow, and terrestrial water storage, enabling diagnosis of both dynamic a S rz and its realized capacity. Applied across hundreds of U.S. catchments over the period 2001–2020, the framework reveals coherent spatial and hydroclimatic patterns, with a S rz peaking in transitional regions where atmospheric demand and water supply are balanced. The realized capacity reflects how belowground water access varies with long‐term hydroclimatic and substrate constraints. We further show that defining storage as a realized quantity through system dynamics improves stability and interpretability under varying observational and structural conditions. Overall, this study demonstrates how hybrid modeling can be used to diagnose ecosystem‐accessible water storage as a latent state, providing a physically consistent and observation‐informed pathway to quantify belowground processes that remain inaccessible to direct measurement and control key land‐atmosphere interactions.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Baseflow Separation Methods Using an Integrated Hydrologic Model in a Snow‐Dominated Watershed
authors: Jihad Othman; Pin Shuai
abstract: Abstract Baseflow constitutes over half of streamflow in mountainous headwaters of the western United States (US), making accurate quantification critical for water resource management. However, traditional baseflow separation methods are often arbitrary and ambiguous, complicating validation. Here, we developed an integrated hydrologic model coupling surface and subsurface flow to quantify baseflow in the Coal Creek watershed, a snow‐dominated catchment in Colorado, US. A model‐agnostic approach was implemented to estimate baseflow from simulated hydrologic exchange fluxes and these estimates were used as a reference to evaluate four common baseflow separation methods: the Pettyjohn and Henning (PH) graphical, United Kingdom Institute of Hydrology (UKIH) graphical, Eckhardt digital filter, and conductance mass balance (CMB) methods. Both the UKIH and Eckhardt methods performed relatively well, with modified Kling‐Gupta Efficiency values of 0.73 and 0.68 and Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency values of 0.59 and 0.71, respectively. However, the UKIH method underperformed during average and dry years, when stream hydrographs exhibit unimodal peaks typical of snow‐dominated catchments. The PH and CMB methods showed poor performance overall: the PH method substantially overestimated baseflow (average baseflow index (BFI) of 85%) owing to its short moving window, while the CMB method underestimated it (average BFI of 38%), potentially due to the exclusion of interflow contributions, compared to a numerically derived BFI of 58%. These findings highlight the utility of integrated hydrologic models as a reference for evaluating baseflow separation methods, particularly in snow‐dominated catchments where graphical and tracer‐based approaches may misrepresent baseflow contributions.

title: Quantifying Vegetation Dependence on Groundwater: Evidence From Northern China's Drylands
authors: Xing LI; Yong Wang; Yong Zhao; Jiaqi Zhai; Fan He; Yuan Liu; Jiaxin Li; Kuan Liu; Tao Wang; Minjian CHEN
abstract: Abstract Groundwater is a critical source for vegetation in drylands, yet the quantification of vegetation dependence on groundwater (VDG) remains underexplored. Understanding this dependence is essential for unraveling vegetation‐groundwater interactions and informing sustainable water resources management in drylands. This study constructed a vegetation response curve to depth to groundwater (DTG) by analyzing the relationship between DTG and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) at the pixel scale. A new method was developed to quantify VDG from the fitted NDVI–DTG response curve, where VDG was defined as the rate of NDVI change per unit change in normalized DTG at the inflection point of the NDVI–DTG response curve. VDG values were obtained for nine representative arid, semi‐arid, and semi‐humid regions in northern China (with an annual precipitation gradient of 200–800 mm). VDG shows pronounced spatial variation across the nine regions, with mean values decreasing from approximately 1.28 in the driest region to approximately 0.24 in the wettest region along the precipitation gradient. A strong negative correlation between annual precipitation (P) and VDG was identified (VDG = 2.08e −0.0037P ), highlighting precipitation as a dominant regulator of VDG across regions. The research provides new empirical evidence for a deeper understanding of the effects of groundwater on vegetation, and also provides strong scientific support for groundwater management and ecological restoration with various annual precipitation amounts.

title: Quantifying Groundwater–Surface Water Exchange on a River Island: A Comparative Analysis of Direct and Indirect Methods
authors: Nayeon Ki; Kyungwon Kwak; Jonghoon Park; Gyeongseo Jeong; Yongmoon Lee; Hanjin Choe; Chung‐Mo Lee
abstract: Abstract Groundwater–surface water exchange is a key hydrological process that governs river water quality and aquatic ecosystems. However, the quantification of such exchange remains uncertain, especially within river island aquifers where exchange processes are highly heterogeneous. In this study, direct seepage meter measurements and indirect Darcy‐based estimates of exchange fluxes were compared under consistent spatiotemporal conditions within the aquifer of Jungsa Island, a river island in the lower West Nakdong River, South Korea. At the downstream low‐permeability site (SP‐3), Darcy‐based exchange fluxes ranged from −2.14 × 10 −5 to 1.15 × 10 −5 m/hr. Owing to these small magnitudes, net intrusion and discharge were not distinguishable. However, seepage meter measurements consistently indicated intrusion of surface water into the island aquifer, with fluxes ranging from −8.46 × 10 −4 to −1.94 × 10 −4 m/hr. At the upstream high‐permeability site (SP‐6), seepage meter measurements captured both transient groundwater discharge during short measurement periods and sustained surface water intrusion during longer measurements. Darcy‐based estimates at this site consistently indicated intrusion, indicating that both methods showed the same flow direction during longer measurements. Consequently, Darcy‐based approaches may underestimate exchange fluxes under low‐permeability conditions. These findings suggest that short‐term monitoring is favorable for capturing immediate, transient flow dynamics, whereas extended continuous measurements help buffer short‐term fluctuations to provide a more representative estimate of daily integrated exchange. Ultimately, by establishing a methodological framework that accounts for localized riverbed heterogeneity, this study provides practical guidelines for optimizing field investigation strategies in complex riparian environments.

title: Phosphorus composition in urban estuarine sediments: similar spatial patterns, distinct seasonal drivers, transformation pathways and risks

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Hydrological Models
authors: Yang Yang; Joseph Janssen; Hoshin Gupta; Ting Fong May Chui
abstract: Abstract The evaluation of hydrological models is essential for both model selection and reliability assessment. However, comparing predictions with observations alone is insufficient to fully characterize model behavior. This limitation is particularly relevant to deep learning (DL) models because of their complex internal structures. In risk‐averse operational settings, water managers require models whose reliability and failure modes have been carefully evaluated because unstable predictions can put critical infrastructure at risk. Motivated by the need to assess model reliability before operational deployment, we introduce and explore adversarial robustness analysis for hydrological modeling and evaluate whether small, targeted perturbations to meteorological forcings induce substantial changes in simulated discharge. We compare a physical‐conceptual model (HBV) with a deep learning‐based model (LSTM) across 1,347 German catchments using perturbations of varying magnitudes generated by the fast gradient sign method (FGSM). We find that FGSM perturbations generally reduce Kling–Gupta efficiency and increase mean squared error. However, widespread catastrophic failures under the specific FGSM perturbations are not observed, and LSTM generally exhibits less performance degradation than HBV. In the examined catchments, changes in the predicted hydrographs and time‐averaged internal model states often vary approximately linearly with perturbation magnitude, providing a compact summary of how errors grow under such perturbations. Similar patterns are observed along random perturbation directions in selected catchments, suggesting that, in those catchments, small input changes produce approximately proportional changes in model output. Overall, these findings characterize local predictive stability under controlled stress tests and motivate future studies of model robustness in real‐world operational settings.

title: Offshore Groundwater Salinization and Flushing in the Canterbury Bight During Glacial‐Interglacial Cycles
authors: Chong Sheng; Christian Hensen; Aaron Micallef; Thomas Müller; Ariel T. Thomas; Mark Schmidt
abstract: Abstract Offshore freshened groundwater (OFG) is a significant yet underexplored component of global water resources, occurring widely along many continental margins. However, its dynamics remain poorly constrained due to limited offshore observations and the absence of robust evaluation models for unambiguous emplacement interpretation. To address this knowledge gap, we integrate existing porewater data and geological constraints from the Canterbury Bight with paleo‐hydrogeochemical modeling to investigate the origin, evolution, and biogeochemical processes related to OFG driven by sea‐level fluctuations. Our simulation results indicate that modern recharge from onshore aquifers contributes only a limited fraction of the present OFG. The majority of OFG has mean groundwater ages of less than ∼300 kyr, suggesting that it mainly originates from local meteoric recharge during sea‐level lowstands since the late Pleistocene. OFG volume and paleo‐submarine groundwater discharge along the continental shelf have varied periodically in response to sea‐level fluctuations throughout glacial‐interglacial cycles. The Canterbury Bight OFG system is currently in a non‐steady state, undergoing gradual salinization by downward intrusion from overlying seawater at an estimated rate of 0.06 cm yr −1 . The long‐term evolution of the OFG system has increased the complexity of biogeochemical processes within shelf sediments through freshwater–seawater mixing. By integrating paleo‐hydrogeological reconstruction, geological archives, and reactive transport modeling, this study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding OFG formation and evolution, advancing beyond previous models focused primarily on salinity.

title: Nationwide sustainability assessment of PFAS treatment in U.S. water utilities
authors: Md. Moshiur Rahman Tushar; Zaki Alam Pushan; Craig Page; Nirupam Aich; Lewis Stetson Rowles
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) pose an unprecedented challenge for US drinking water systems as new national regulations mandate their removal. While granular activated carbon (GAC) and ion exchange (IX) resins are widely applied, their economic and environmental sustainability under diverse real-world conditions remains uncertain. Here we leverage a quantitative sustainable design framework (integrated techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment) to evaluate GAC and IX performance across utilities nationwide. Through uncertainty and sensitivity analyses, we identify utility size, water types (e.g., groundwater and surface water), and PFAS chain length as the dominant drivers of cost and environmental impacts. IX consistently shows lower global warming potential than GAC, though treatment of short-chain PFAS significantly increases costs. Water quality, especially total organic carbon, affects treatment performance and can change cost and environmental impacts for GAC. Results highlight disproportionate burdens on small and rural systems and the trade-offs inherent in technology selection. This work provides actionable insight for utilities and policymakers, enabling more equitable and sustainable strategies for meeting emerging PFAS standards.

title: Molecularly engineered zwitterionic‑fluorinated hydrogel electrolyte for durable Ah-level zinc-ion batteries
authors: Bingyan Guo; Junfeng Li; Zhexuan Liu; Xiao Xiao; 宋业新; Zhiyang Zheng; Xiongwei Zhong; Xiaomin Xu; Yang Su; Qingjin Fu; Guangmin Zhou
abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries are considered suitable candidates for grid storage but suffer from Zn dendrites and water-induced side reactions. Incorporating appropriate hydrophobic moieties into hydrogel electrolytes is an effective strategy to reduce water activity and widen the electrochemical stability window. To further advance this molecular design framework and enable precise interphase modulation, we report a molecularly engineered zwitterionic-fluorinated hydrogel electrolyte. Within the polymer network, the rationally introduced hydrophobic fluoroalkyl moieties (–CH2CF3) strengthen hydrogen bonds between hydrophilic units and water, thereby reducing water activity and mitigating parasitic reactions. Meanwhile, the zincophilic zwitterionic units (–SO3–, –N+(CH3)3) facilitate rapid and directional Zn2+ transport, with a Zn2+ transference number of 0.76. These tailored functional groups synergistically promote the in-situ formation of an organic–inorganic solid electrolyte interphase, enabling Zn negative electrode stability, achieving over 900 h of Zn plating/stripping at 5.0 mA cm–2 and 5.0 mAh cm–2. Furthermore, Zn | |MnO2 pouch cells incorporating this electrolyte deliver a capacity of ~1 Ah and operate for over 700 h, indicating the potential of this electrolyte for large-scale energy storage applications. Aqueous zinc-ion batteries promise safe energy storage but suffer from dendrites and side reactions. Here, authors engineer a zwitterionic fluorinated hydrogel electrolyte to suppress these issues, enabling durable, dendrite free, Ah-level pouch cells.

title: Modeling Incentive‐Driven Cooperation in Agricultural Water Use Under Unequal Withdrawal Condition
authors: Jiheun Kim; Jeongwoo Hwang; Seung Beom Seo
abstract: Abstract Water allocation has long been framed as a general optimization problem in which users compete for a finite resource, leading much of the existing literature to adopt a top‐down perspective on how water should be distributed among users. However, in practice, water withdrawals may also be influenced by physical access and operational arrangements, such as direct abstraction from river channels through intake facilities for agricultural and industrial use. In such systems, disparities may arise between institutional allocation principles and effective access to water during shortage conditions, potentially creating asymmetric impacts among upstream, midstream, and downstream stakeholders. This study quantifies these impact asymmetries across river locations and evaluates stage‐based intake restriction strategies designed to mitigate inequitable outcomes during droughts. The proposed framework is applied to the Yeongsan River Basin in southwestern Korea through computational experiments to demonstrate how drought‐stage‐based intake regulations can improve both net profit and equity among stakeholders. A game‐theoretic approach is further employed to assess the potential for compensation across Pareto‐optimal solutions by examining whether the additional gains generated under cooperation are sufficient to offset stakeholder losses relative to the non‐cooperative baseline. The analysis is extended to projected scenarios of intensified climatic and socio‐economic droughts to assess the robustness of the proposed policies under future stress conditions. Through this approach, the study introduces a generalized framework for identifying water allocation policies that reconcile efficiency, equity, and sustainability under institutional and hydrologic constraints.

title: In the Age of AI—Are National Models and Data Sets Still Important for Stream Flow Prediction?
authors: Brett Snider; Ehsan Roshani
abstract: Abstract Accurate streamflow prediction is critical for effective water resource management, and recent advances in deep learning and multi‐basin data sets have significantly improved model skill. Global deep‐learning models, trained on thousands of catchments have demonstrated strong generalization across diverse climates and continents. However, these models rely solely on globally available meteorological inputs, potentially overlooking the value of nationally developed data sets with enhanced regional accuracy. In this study, we assess the benefit of using Canada's high‐resolution national reanalysis data set (CaSR) in long short‐term memory (LSTM) models for streamflow prediction. We compare model performance using different meteorological forcings, global (ERA5‐Land), continental (Daymet), national (CaSR), and a combined “Complete” model, across over 1,000 Canadian stream gauges. Model performance is evaluated using the Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling‐Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and related metrics. We also benchmark our best‐performing model against Google's global LSTM streamflow model at 412 Canadian gauges. Results show that national‐scale deep‐learning models using CaSR outperforms deep‐learning models using only global or continental inputs. The Complete model achieved the highest performance, with a median KGE 0.886−exceeding the 0.839 achieved by Google's global model within Canada. These findings suggest that nationally trained models using a wide array of inputs, including national meteorological data sets, can outperform state‐of‐the‐art global deep‐learning models that do not use such data when applied within their region of origin. For countries with dense observational networks and distinct hydrological regimes, investing in national data sets and models can enhance deep‐learning model prediction accuracy, leading to improved resilience to climate extremes and local water management decisions.

title: HydroDiffusion: Diffusion‐Based Probabilistic Streamflow Forecasting With a State Space Backbone
authors: Yihan Wang; Annan Yu; Lujun Zhang; Charuleka Varadharajan; N. Benjamin Erichson
abstract: Abstract Recent advances have introduced diffusion models for probabilistic streamflow forecasting, demonstrating strong early flood‐warning skill. However, current implementations rely on Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) backbones and discrete‐time diffusion formulations. This leaves unresolved whether more advanced sequence‐modeling architectures and continuous‐time diffusion formulations can improve probabilistic streamflow forecasting. In this study, we developed HydroDiffusion, a diffusion‐based probabilistic forecasting framework integrating a decoder‐only state space model (SSM) backbone with a continuous‐time score‐based diffusion formulation. HydroDiffusion is evaluated across 531 watersheds in the contiguous United States (CONUS) in the CAMELS data set. We benchmark HydroDiffusion against two diffusion baselines with LSTM backbones, as well as the recently proposed Diffusion‐based Runoff Model (DRUM). Results show that HydroDiffusion achieves the strongest nowcast accuracy when driven by observed meteorological forcings. Moreover, HydroDiffusion delivers higher deterministic and probabilistic forecast skill than its LSTM‐based counterpart in operational forecasting. Attribution analysis further reveals that the SSM backbone excels in humid, densely vegetated, storage‐dominated watersheds with strong hydrologic memory, while its advantage becomes limited in arid regions and hydrologically complex systems such as karst and prairie pothole basins. These results establish HydroDiffusion as an effective generative modeling framework for medium‐range streamflow forecasting, providing both a new modeling benchmark and a foundation for future research on probabilistic hydrologic prediction at continental scales.

title: Hydraulic Barrier Optimization Using Random‐Walk Particle Tracking in Heterogeneous Media: Effects of Dispersion, Particle Discretization and Algorithmic Initialization
authors: Daniele Pedretti
abstract: Abstract Hydraulic barriers (HBs) are commonly used for solute plume containment in polluted aquifers. Their long‐term sustainability depends on minimizing the cumulative pumping rate, , required to ensure plume capture. Lagrangian random‐walk particle tracking (RWPT) is an effective approach for simulating advective‐dispersive transport to wells. However, as this method typically requires a large number of particles, , RWPT‐based simulation–optimization (SO) can be computationally demanding. This work presents an SO framework that couples a warm‐start genetic algorithm with parallel RWPT to identify minimal pumping rates for HB containment in a computationally efficient manner. The framework was applied in a Monte Carlo study using stochastic hydraulic conductivity fields, with ranging from to . Results showed that optimal values were jointly conditioned by transport processes, particle discretization, and algorithmic initialization. Under advection‐only transport, was nearly insensitive to . In contrast, when local dispersion was included, and its variability increased with . The influence of particle discretization depended strongly on the adopted recovery criterion, becoming substantially weaker when incomplete particle recovery was allowed. Neglecting local dispersion can therefore underestimate pumping requirements, particularly under stringent recovery criteria and increasing particle resolution. Warm‐start initialization generally identified lower solutions than cold initialization while also reducing computational time. These findings demonstrate that particle discretization, local dispersion and the recovery criterion should be considered explicitly when optimizing HBs, and that warm‐start strategies can substantially improve computational efficiency in RWPT‐based SO workflows.

title: High-entropy enabled two-dimensional ferroelectricity and memristive synapses in van der Waals layered materials
authors: Ning Sun; Xu Han; Weishen Li; Bowen Zhang; Xiangjiang Dong; Ming Lei; Yehua Yang; Yuan Zhang; Wei‐Hsiang Huang; Chih‐Wen Pao; Yunhui Huang; Jianchun Xu; Ruge Quhe; Weimin Wang; Kai Huang
abstract: Two-dimensional ferroelectric materials offer opportunities for ultrathin non-volatile electronics, but their development is limited by stringent structural requirements for intrinsic polarity. Here we show that high-entropy engineering can induce switchable polarization in centrosymmetric van der Waals materials. By introducing configurational disorder into layered metal phosphorus trisulfides, we synthesize (MnFeCoNi)1−xCdxPS3 single crystals exhibiting electric-field-induced polar states and ferroelectric-like switching at ±0.5 V, with a transition temperature up to 523 K. Combined calculations and characterizations reveal that polarization originates from electric-field-driven Cd2+ migration enabled by lattice distortions and heterogeneous coordination environments. This migration-mediated mechanism differs from conventional ferroelectric models and enables non-volatile neuromorphic functions, including long-term potentiation and bidirectional weight modulation. This work establishes high-entropy engineering as a strategy for manipulating ion migration dynamics in two-dimensional layered materials, opening a pathway toward emergent ferroelectric-like states beyond the conventional requirement of non-centrosymmetric structures. Two-dimensional ferroelectrics are often constrained by stringent structural requirements for intrinsic polarity. Sun et al. demonstrate that high-entropy engineering enables switchable polarization in centrosymmetric van der Waals materials, offering a potential pathway toward emergent ferroelectric-like states.

title: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
authors: Lee Haverson; Lisa Mignanelli; Uwe Schneidewind; Stefan Krause
abstract: Abstract Previous research has pinpointed storm events as significant potential controls of microplastic (MP) export to the oceans. Hysteretic behavior of discharge ( Q )—concentration (c) relationships for suspended sediment (SS) and solutes has been found important in understanding the dynamic activation and transport of these substances, additionally providing better estimations of long‐term loads. Due to limited availability of high frequency event‐based MP concentration data their potential hysteretic behavior has not been studied, leaving a substantial knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport mechanisms controlling MP activation and retention within catchments. We pioneer the use of high frequency MP data collected during a storm event revealing the time variable activation of different sources and transport mechanisms within a peri‐urban catchment. Surface water samples were collected before, during and after the event and combined with discharge and turbidity data to quantify MP concentrations and fluxes. Analysis of the hysteretic behavior of the Q‐c relationship revealed a clockwise hysteresis pattern with MP concentration peaking before Q , suggesting potential MP supply limitation for the sampled event. Regression analysis indicates Q to be the primary driving force promoting MP flux, with strong correlations between Q and MP concentration in rising and falling limbs. A strong Q ‐ turbidity relationship was observed only in the rising limb, potentially indicating spatial differences in the sources of SS and MPs transported in the falling limb. Total MP flux increased by 17–217 times to that of baseflow, highlighting the significance of often‐overlooked dynamics when calculating yearly MP flux.

title: Head-to-tail assembled borphyrins for solid-state lithium extraction
authors: Ehsan Hamzehpoor; Seiya Ota; Suprio Chowdhury; Zongzhe Li; Alyssa Yeung; Rhianna A. Parcon; Raksha Kandel; Brian O. Patrick; Mark J. MacLachlan
abstract: Abstract Lithium is a critical mineral for advancing greener technologies. Extraction of lithium ions (Li⁺) from sea salt, minerals, and waste is important, but has been hindered by the lack of extraction methods that offer both high selectivity and strong lithium affinity. Here, we report a dioxaborole-linked, head-to-tail assembled macrocycle – termed borphyrin – featuring a rigid cavity with a 16-crown-4-like configuration. This molecule exhibits strong affinity for lithium and high selectivity over competing cations under dry solid-liquid extraction conditions, owing to its narrow binding cavity and planar macrocyclic core. Borphyrin enabled the extraction of lithium from crystalline solids of ether-insoluble salts, as well as selective extraction of Li⁺ from dried mixed-salt matrices containing alkali, alkaline earth and transition-metal salts. These results establish borphyrin as a potential molecular platform for selective lithium recognition and solid-liquid lithium extraction.

title: From Hazard to Resource: A Screening‐Level Assessment of Glacial Lake Hydropower Potential and Development Suitability in the Poiqu River Basin, Central Himalaya
authors: Jiyao Zhu; Guoxiong Zheng; Guoqing Zhang; Wenfeng Chen; Yan Zhong; Simon Allen; Dongfeng Li; Ye Yuan; Yihua Zhong; Shijin Wang; Xiaojun Bu; Markus Stoffel
abstract: Abstract Climate warming accelerates glacier retreat and glacial lake expansion, creating hydropower opportunities while increasing flood hazards. Despite extensive research on glacial lake hazards, assessments of hydropower potential and development suitability remain limited. Here, we quantify the theoretical hydropower potential of 37 glacial lakes in the Poiqu river basin, central Himalaya, by integrating multi‐scenario climate projections with annual lake water budget reconstruction to estimate hydropower‐relevant inflow across four operational stages during 2025–2100 and by deriving available hydraulic heads through hierarchical river network and topographic gradient analyses. We develop a multi‐criteria framework to evaluate environmental, technical, and economic suitability and prioritize lakes. Across four climate scenarios, basin‐wide mean annual generation is projected at about 212.8 GWhr yr −1 during Stage I (risk mitigation, 2025–2030), followed by about 200.6, 197.0, and 194.3 GWhr yr −1 during Stages II–IV (adaptive generation, 2031–2100), respectively. Paqupuco is identified as the top‐priority site, with annual generation potential of about 14.3 GWhr yr −1 and a suitability score of 80.6. At the regional screening scale, modeled operations could reduce the maximum storage of high‐risk lakes, such as Gangxico and Galongco, to about 71% of their initial capacities. Sensitivity analyses indicate that basin‐wide estimates and leading candidates are broadly stable under the tested water budget and weighting assumptions. By linking hydropower resource assessment with climate‐adaptive hazard governance, this study provides a regional screening framework for jointly evaluating clean energy opportunities and glacial lake outburst flood mitigation in glacierized mountain regions.

title: Four Decades of Reach‐Scale Declines in Total Phosphorus Across the Yellow River Basin Driven by Vegetation Restoration and Dam Impoundment
authors: Cihong Fang; Dongfeng Li; Shang Tian; Guowangchen Liu; Anmeng Sha; Yan Li
abstract: Abstract Phosphorus (P) is a finite resource fundamental to terrestrial and aquatic productivity. However, excessive P transfer from land to rivers threatens food production and degrades water quality. Systematic analyses of multidecadal total phosphorus (TP) variation in large river basins remain challenging because of incomplete and non‐uniform observational data. Here, we develop a potentially transferable and generalizable framework combining remote sensing and machine learning to reconstruct long‐term and reach‐scale TP variation in the Yellow River Basin from 1986 to 2024, based on synchronous multimodal and in situ data ( N = 1,490). The results confirm that the framework can reliably estimate TP concentration, achieving Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency = 0.71 and root mean squared error = 27.1 μg L −1 on the test set. TP concentration shows a significant temporal decline in 55% of river reaches; spatial heterogeneity is evident, with concentrations in the middle reaches declining most rapidly at 4.1 μg L −1 per decade. However, TP flux (TPF) exhibits a U‐shaped temporal trajectory, increasing after 2015 as river discharge rises; the spatial gradient follows a hump‐shaped pattern, characterized by a peak of 2,094 t yr −1 at Tongguan. Vegetation restoration reduces land‐to‐river TP export, and dam impoundment impedes in‐stream TP transport, both of which largely account for the declines in TP concentration in the Yellow River Basin. This study proposes a potentially generalizable framework for riverine TP reconstruction at high spatial resolution over multiple decades and provides new insights into the anthropogenic impact on TP dynamics in big river systems.

title: Flood Types Reveal Non‐Stationarity in Flood Peaks Masked by Annual‐Maximum Series
authors: Svenja Fischer; Gregor Laaha; Farhana Sweeta Fitriana
abstract: Abstract Flood frequency analysis (FFA) forms the basis of many hydrological assessments and practical design calculations. Traditionally, FFA is based on the assumptions of stationary distributions and homogeneous samples. These assumptions are questionable in light of climate change and the wide variety of hydrological processes that lead to flooding. Furthermore, these assumptions can obscure important insights, including process‐specific changes. In this study, we develop a process‐aware, non‐stationary mixture model that combines type‐specific distributions with time‐varying parameters. An application to more than 600 catchments across Europe shows that the various flood types change differently over time. Heavy rainfall floods at many locations in Europe (e.g., the Alps and UK) are increasing significantly, whereas snowmelt floods are decreasing. In conventional models, these findings are obscured by the combined analysis of opposing trends, and trends are often not recognised. This causes design quantiles, for example, for a 100‐year return period, to be underestimated by about 15% on average in many regions of Europe when non‐stationary, type‐specific distributions are not used. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating process understanding into FFA to improve design‐flood estimation and our understanding of changing flood‐generating processes.

title: Exploring Climate Change Effects on Concurrent Floods and Concurrent Droughts via Statistical Deep Learning
authors: C. J. R. Murphy‐Barltrop; J. Richards; Benjamin Poschlod; A. Sasse; Jakob Zscheischler A
abstract: Abstract Concurrent floods and concurrent droughts in nearby catchments pose challenges to risk assessment and water management. Climate change is affecting extremely high and low discharge, but the complex interplay between changes in individual catchments, and in the dependence across catchments, make it difficult to provide accurate assessments of the occurrence probabilities of concurrent extremes. In this work, we use a contemporary statistical deep learning model to capture concurrent river floods and droughts in four catchments in the Upper Danube basin, based on discharge simulated by a hydrological model driven with large ensemble climate model output. The statistical model is able to accurately capture the tail behavior of the simulated discharge, which we assess by making use of the large available sample. We subsequently use our statistical model to study changes in joint tail behavior of discharge over time, finding that both compound flooding and drought‐like conditions are becoming increasingly likely toward the end of the 21st century under a high‐emission scenario. In particular, our results highlight that changes in the dependence structure of extremes strongly contribute to the detected changes, an aspect that would be difficult to capture with traditional approaches. This work paves the way for highly flexible, general inference on compound extremes in hydrological applications, and demonstrates key advantages of using statistical deep learning in this setting.

title: Evolution of Institutional Dynamics in Water Resource Governance in the Yellow River Basin
authors: Chee Hui Lai; Jianshi Zhao
abstract: Abstract Many large river basins, such as the Yellow River Basin (YRB) of China, have undergone water governance transformations to resolve long‐standing and emerging challenges. However, how newly introduced water‐related laws and regulations structurally transform internal institutional dynamics—the functions and interactions of institutional elements (e.g., governance rules and actors) within the governance system—and ultimately contribute to improved governance performance remains poorly understood. This knowledge gap limits our ability to explain why some water governance reforms succeed while others fail. Therefore, this paper examines how new water‐related legislation alters governance rules, redefines institutional roles and interactions among basin actors, and drives changes in water governance mode and performance, taking the YRB as a case. To analyze institutional dynamics, we propose an approach that integrates Sankey diagrams, institutional grammar, the rule typology of the institutional analysis and development framework, and a set of rule‐based governance indicators. This approach can decompose, connect, and trace institutional effects generated by legislative variation. Five national‐level legislative documents that have fundamentally transformed the YRB's water governance over recent decades are analyzed. The basin's governance mode evolved from fragmented (1987–1997) to centralized uncoordinated (1998–2001) and ultimately centralized coordinated (2006 onward). The interplay of legislative documents, institutionalized areas (e.g., water allocation and flow regulation), governance rule types (e.g., action‐specific and target‐specific rules), power distribution (e.g., centralization and decentralization), and coordination mechanisms (e.g., prior consultation and joint operation), drives the evolution of water governance modes. These findings offer insights for institutional designs in large river basins worldwide.

title: Evaluating SWOT Satellite Data With Gage Information in the United States and Canada
authors: Merritt E. Harlan; David Michael Bjerklie; Jack R. Eggleston; Dongmei Feng; Ryan Riggs; Fiona B Bennitt; Cécile Cazals; Robert W. Dudley; Michael Durand; Elisa Friedmann; Colin Joseph Gleason; Justin Toby Minear; Hind Oubanas; Tamlin M. Pavelsky; C. Stuurman
abstract: Abstract The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite mission represents a transformative approach to water resources management, offering high‐resolution data on water‐surface elevations (WSE) and extents. This study evaluates SWOT WSE accuracy in the United States and Canada with in situ streamgage and lake and reservoir gage data. We compare SWOT Level 2 Hydrology data products (Version D) to in situ timeseries of WSE on 335,531 paired observations across 2,629 gages. SWOT data accuracy and temporal coverage are explored as functions of various SWOT quality filters. After applying a standard set of defined filters and thresholds to compare paired measurements of SWOT and in situ observations (both referenced to the Earth Gravitational Model 2008), we find 1‐σ (68th percentile) absolute differences of 20 and 11 cm, and median biases of 2.8 and 0.1 cm, for filtered river node and lake data, respectively. River reach and lake comparisons may be biased due to scale mismatches between in situ point‐based data and spatially averaged SWOT data. Applying SWOT data quality filters improved median paired elevation R 2 between unfiltered and filtered data from 0.12 to 0.92 across all reach, node, and lake observations. Overall, we find that 60.0% and 73.8% of all paired SWOT node and lake WSE observations that satisfy SWOT‐observable criteria (ice‐free observations from sufficiently large waterbodies within the SWOT cross track range) have elevations within 25 cm of reported gage observations. These comparisons also provide a baseline benchmark that can help inform continued SWOT algorithm refinement.

title: Diagnosing Latent Storage Representations in LSTM Reservoir Release Policies
authors: M. Chen; Jonathan D. Herman
abstract: Abstract The influence of reservoirs on the water cycle introduces significant uncertainty for hydrologic prediction. The representation of reservoirs in hydrologic models ideally must be accurate, interpretable, and transferable across sites. Recent studies have highlighted the potential for data‐driven methods, including long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks, to accurately capture reservoir releases. However, the performance of LSTM models of reservoir releases has not yet been diagnosed on a large‐sample data set to understand whether their accuracy is physically justified. This study evaluates the ability of LSTMs to represent reservoir release policies across the continental U.S., leveraging the recently developed ResOpsUS data set. In particular, we focus on whether LSTMs can infer a latent storage representation without being provided observed storage as input. We find that in many cases the LSTM succeeds in encoding physically interpretable storage dynamics in its internal states, despite measurement errors in the data. However, the model accuracy is only weakly related to the strength of the learned storage representation; instead, it is log‐linearly related to the degree of regulation. In addition, LSTMs struggle to generalize storage dynamics and learned policies in space with pooled training. This study contributes to the growing literature on interpreting deep learning models of human‐hydrologic systems.

title: Demand-side strategies unlock gigaton-scale GHG mitigation beyond supply-side limits in the global lithium-ion battery supply chain
authors: Haiwei Zhou; Wen Li; Peng Wang; Prakash J. Singh; Fanran Meng
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) underpin the clean energy transition, yet their supply chains remain carbon-intensive and risk becoming a major source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Supply-side decarbonization is therefore crucial, but can it curb emissions fast enough as demand grows globally? Combining dynamic material flow analysis and life cycle assessment, we show that annual GHG emissions from the global LIB supply chain could rise more than 10-fold over 2024–2050. While supply-side strategies lower GHG intensity substantially, cutting cumulative emissions by 3.5–4.7 Gt CO 2 -eq, they face mitigation limits from technical ceilings, deployment dynamics, and cross-strategy interactions. Demand-side strategies are essential to further constrain supply-chain emissions, unlocking 6.0–7.2 Gt CO 2 -eq of cumulative mitigation beyond what supply-side decarbonization alone can achieve. Demand-side strategies also consistently lower broader environmental impacts (e.g., land occupation and human toxicity) that respond weakly to supply-side decarbonization, extending their value beyond climate mitigation.

title: Deep Learning‐Based Fusion of Hydrodynamic Model and Remote Sensing Observation for Mapping the Inundation Dynamics in Large Wetlands Under Changing Environment
authors: Siyang Yao; Siyang Yao; Ligang Xu; Ying Le; Dong Liao; Jiang Wu; Siyu Wan
abstract: Abstract Wetlands play a crucial role in maintaining the global ecosystem balance, and determining the inundation dynamics is of great significance for understanding wetland ecosystems. Hydrodynamic models are effective tools for mapping the inundation dynamics; however, they are affected by uncertainties arising from environmental changes, including anthropogenic pressures and land cover modifications, especially in large wetlands. To overcome hydrodynamic model limitations, this study integrated a hydrodynamic module, a remote sensing module, and a deep learning fusion module to develop an efficient approach for mapping the inundation dynamics. This approach was applied in the Poyang Lake Wetland in China, a vital conservation wetland in the Ramsar Convention. The effectiveness of this approach was verified by comparing the simulated inundation dynamics of the hydrodynamic model during the dry season. We found that the performance of the hydrodynamic model was relatively poor. In particular, the performance in the sub‐lake area was significantly inferior than the other zone, with an overall accuracy (OA, dimensionless, ranging from 0 to 1) of only 0.63–0.66. The proposed approach in this study exhibited better performance, especially in the sub‐lake area, with an OA increasing to 0.82–0.92. Furthermore, the hydrodynamic model tended to overestimate the inundation time, with the median overestimated time reaching 42–50 days. Our study provides a transferable framework that can improve the accuracy of wetland hydrological monitoring under changing environment, contribute to maintaining the ecological integrity and stability.

title: Cross-border electricity tariffs undermine power system efficiency, decarbonization and reliability in North America
authors: Siyuan Wang; Fengqi You
abstract: The United States and Canada share an interconnected electricity system where cross-border trade lowers costs, supports low-carbon generation and balances supply and demand during stress. Tariff disputes risk costlier or curtailed electricity imports, yet the system-wide consequences remain unclear. Here we show, using ten years of New York electricity-market data and power-system simulations, that tariffs on Canadian electricity reduce imports, raise prices, lower economic welfare and increase carbon emissions by replacing hydropower- and nuclear-rich imports with fossil-fuel generation. Tariffs above about 55% on Ontario imports, or about 90% when extended to Quebec, nearly eliminate affected imports under historical market conditions. Reduced access to Canadian power shrinks operating reserves, which provide spare capacity during unexpected shortages, increases reliance on oil-fired plants during summer peaks, and raises the risk of forced power cuts during severe winter disruptions. Open cross-border electricity trade therefore supports cost efficiency, decarbonization and grid resilience. Analysis of a decade of New York power-market data and simulations shows that tariffs on Canadian electricity imports could raise prices and emissions, diminish economic benefits, and weaken grid reliability during peak demand and extreme weather.
